thread.title: Cirrus Logic Investors: Navigating Through Apple's iPhone Uncertainties - Cirrus Logic, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRUS)

author: Patient Tech Investor
title: Cirrus Logic Investors: Navigating Through Apple's iPhone Uncertainties - Cirrus Logic, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRUS)
text:
Our Past History Over the past few years, we have made several revenue and earnings projections for Cirrus Logic ( CRUS ). In general, our errors relate with huge misses in guessing iPhone and Galaxy phone unit sales. For example, we badly missed the so-called super cycle unit sales for iPhone by 20-30 million units, which was approximately a dollar or more in earnings.
Instead of guessing unit sales for phones, we are including ranges beginning with the March quarter 2019. Interested investors may draw their own conclusions. We have fixed a few factors, including gross margins at 51%, tax rates at 17%, average Apple ( AAPL ) ASP at $4.85, and the share count averaged at 60 million. We are moving the gross margin up one percentage point because Cirrus continues to broadcast a significant amount of new Android revenue. Android parts tend to be catalog, which at least in the past yielded higher margins. Unless Apple changes its approach, we don't expect unit growth with its iPhone product at least through September 2020.
Coming Growth During its most recent conference, Cirrus's CEO, Jason Rhode, commented, "So, amps and haptic [are] kind of the nearest-term drivers of growth for us going forward." Speaking of the amplifier, Rhode added, "So, we’ve already seen some shipping, but we expect a significantly larger contribution from those as we pursue next year." When referring to Wolfson Microelectronics, the CEO continued, "And in fact, a lot of the products that we see being viable parts of our growth path for next year are directly coming out of that - coming out of that acquisition." Beginning next year, Cirrus expects to begin selling a lot more amplifier-based parts into the Android market. Typical ASPs will range between $1 and $1.75.
A New 10% Customer The company continues to reiterate it expects a new 10% customer to appear in the March 2019 quarter. The low quarter in the past few years was June 2018 at $250 million in revenue. We are reasonable certain that no other company except Apple has had more than $25 million within the last few years and that Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) will become the second 10% customer.
Looking back at recent history, we believe that Samsung's quarterly revenue was significantly less than $25 million. Since the Cirrus and Wolfson merger, its business with Samsung has changed significantly. Cirrus now sells a less expensive codec into approximately two-thirds of the Galaxy S series and Note phones. This year, Samsung is expected to sell approximately 30 million units of S and an undetermined number of Notes, probably 10-15 million, a smaller number compared to past years. We have reason to believe that the codec is approximately a $1.5 part generating $15 million or less per quarter.
With some history, we can estimate how much other revenue Samsung might generate for Cirrus. During 2015 and the first quarter of 2016, Cirrus had two 10% customers. One of the two, Samsung, generated $38 million, $50 million, $50 million, $38 million, and $31 million, respectively. Total revenue for Cirrus during that period ranged from $230 million to $350. The Samsung percentage ranged from 11 percent to 18 percent. Between 2105 and early 2016, Cirrus supplied Samsung a higher-priced codec valued somewhere between $2.5 and $3 into all of the Galaxy S series and Note phones because a newly released Qualcomm ( QCOM ) main processing chip failed. In 2016, Qualcomm regained back a third of the Galaxy business for shipments mainly into the United States. In early 2017, Cirrus noted that it had lost some ASP to an unnamed vendor (known publicly to be Samsung). As noted above, the ASP probably dropped to a $1.5. Note: Cirrus's lowest flagship codec is valued at $1.5.
Additional unit sales issues have impacted Cirrus's revenue with Samsung. A recent report states , "Samsung has struggled with "weaker-than-projected sales" of its Galaxy S9 smartphones, according to Bloomberg , which have reportedly sold the lowest of any flagship Samsung smartphone since 2012's Galaxy S3 with expected shipments of 31 million units this year. The Samsung Galaxy S7 has reportedly been the company's most-popular smartphone today, having sold around 50 million units."
A ballpark calculation can give us some idea about how much other business Cirrus may have with Samsung. The peak revenue year with the South Korean company yielded $50 million. Cirrus lost one-third of the business, perhaps 40% of the ASP, and Galaxy phones are roughly 25% lower in sales. Starting with our first guess of $45 million times 0.66 times 0.6 times 0.75 equals $15 million. We think that Cirrus had approximately $5 million in other business, bringing the quarterly total to roughly $20 million.
Cirrus's Samsung story doesn't end with the premium phones, but rather continues with its mid-range opportunities. "One problem: the premium segment on Android isn't very big and is slipping downward in terms of price and performance. Samsung flat out told its investors, given the disappointing sales of its flagship Galaxy S9, that it would be concentrating more on selling middle tier phones like its Galaxy J series . Rather than using Qualcomm's fastest premium chips, these phones use middle-tier Snapdragons or even Samsung's own Exynos chips." (Source: Apple Insider ) Expect Cirrus to provide the codec where Exynos chips are used. If Samsung decides to build all its own mid-range chip sets, Cirrus will win big. The South Korean company sales approximately 75 million phones a quarter, of which approximately 60%, or roughly 30 million, mid-range phones will eventually be a marketing target for Cirrus. We aren't sure what this next year will bring in terms of mid-range, but mid-tier ASPs as shown below starting with a haptic chip and one amplifier is $1.00 to a full complement (one haptic, two amplifiers and one codec is $3.00).
Over the next few years, mid-range opportunities are expected to explode.
For the South Korean company in the March quarter, we expect Cirrus to win all of the amplifiers and a haptic chip inside all of the new Galaxy S phones. The total ASP is approximately $1.50-1.75. With Cirrus's quarterly revenues generally in the $300-400 million, Samsung has to generate at least $15-25 million additional revenue to reach 10%. With unit sales of 10-15 million of Samsung flagship phones a quarter, Cirrus's revenue from this win adds just that. Is more coming from mid-range phones this year? We aren't sure, but we do know it is probable. Note: Cirrus announced a major haptic product addition, one which supports always on (AWO), several conferences ago. We suspect that new Samsung revenue will increase by at least $20 million a quarter at slightly higher margins.
New Screen Mid-Range Phone Trend Begins in 2019 Although we aren't including Samsung mid-range phone opportunities, an article in DigiTimes outlines a new trend which opens up significant opportunities for Cirrus. "Smartphone vendors intend to promote their all-screen models in 2019 to boost their unit sales amid stagnant global demand for smartphones. With all-screen smartphones adopting TDDI (touch and display driver integration) chip solutions, TDDI chip demand is set to grow robustly next year, according to industry sources." (Source: Tech Investor News )
China In a recent conference, Cirrus announced it was shipping product to the 3th-largest OEM. That would be Huawei . The top Chinese OEMs include Huawei, Xiaomi, OPPO and VIVO. We don't expect Cirrus to win with Xiaomi given the latter's cut-throat pricing practices to gain market share. Still, between the other three companies, approximately 100 million a quarter of phones are sold. Again, at 60% within Cirrus's target, that represents 60 million a quarter. Cirrus isn't expecting any of these companies to become 10% anytime soon, but we know that NXP Semiconductors' ( NXPI ) business in China is targeted. During this and coming years, significant ramps will happen with Chinese OEMs. For the coming year, without better information, we are adding a nominal $7 million per quarter beginning in the June quarter.
Headsets In March, Cirrus announced that it was "enabling continuously adaptive ANC in retail headsets with the two largest smartphone OEMs in the world (Samsung and Apple)." (Source: Cirrus Logic Letter to Shareholders Q4 FY18 ) The same letter contained this comment, "Design activity is healthy and we have multiple customer engagements for both wired and wireless digital headsets and adaptors that are targeting inbox and accessory products." This leaves us confused when comparing with a note in the most recent conference comment , "And so that’s becoming kind of more of an accessory business than what we had originally thought would maybe be an [inbox] opportunity but that’s okay." This doesn't dis-include a Galaxy product with an in-the-box approach, but adds uncertainty. One article referenced the analog port in the Galaxy phone will disappear in either the September release of the Note or with the S11 in March 2020. The new phones will supply a single dongle with the change. We are adding revenue with the Note in September with it using a USB-C port and dongle valued for Cirrus at $1. We believe that customers wanting a digital headset will be able to purchase an accessory with a Cirrus part. We also expect Samsung to offer an active noise-canceling (ANC) headset valued at $80 retail to match up with the digital interface. Cirrus's content, depending on whether it includes Cirrus's own microphones, would range between $2.5 and $5. We believe it makes sense for this part to include Cirrus microphones. Possible unit sales might range in the 5-10 million per year, or $15-$50 million in revenue. The South Korean company may also have a wireless headset solution available. Although additional Samsung headset revenue could be significantly higher, we are only adding $8 million a quarter beginning in September.
"On November 8th Patently Apple posted a first patent report titled "Apple's latest Over-the-Ear Headphones Patent covers Noise Cancellation and Five-Mic Voice Beam forming Clarity." (Source: Patently ) We suspect that Cirrus will provide all the mics and ANC chip for an ASP near $5. Analysts' best guess for release is November 2019. Volume is undetermined, but in our view, it will be less than 5 million a year. Beginning in the December quarter of 2019, we are adding 5 million a quarter in revenue.
Revenue and Earnings Projections with the Light On The following tables include the revenue expectations based on two possible iPhone unit sales for the March through December quarters of 2019. Profits are calculated as (Total Revenue * Margin - Cost) * (1-tax rate)). All monetary numbers and iPhone unit sales are in millions.

Each $0.15 decrease in ASP represents approximately 3.4% lower revenue before new business is added. This $0.15 equates to $20 million in lower profits, or $0.33 a share. For example: the profit for iPhones with ASPs of $4.7 would range between $4.4 and $3.9.
We also understand that Apple will continue to over- order in the September quarter. Actual results for September will be greater and for December will be less.
Revenue and Earnings Projections with the Light Off During the last conference, CEO Rhode commented with confidence that the company would make significant dents into its reliance on Apple. No one is certain what a significant dent means - not even Cirrus, in our view - but management must have something in mind. We believe that the quarters in 2015 with two 10% customers gives a hint. Apple dropped to the mid-60s during that period. From a calculation standpoint, with Apple representing something ranged in the 60s, we can calculate other revenue growth by beginning with the company's revenue divided by its future hypothetical percentage.
Below is included a table showing possible future revenues. The numbers are significantly higher than those shown in the above table. What could drive those numbers? Two very possible sources are major wins with China OEMs and Samsung's mid-range. With the later, we included nothing, and yet, we know something is coming. With the former, we included a very small percentage of the potential.

At an average possible ASP of $1.5 per phone, total revenue for these two opportunity reaches $500-600 million. It seems to us that Cirrus's history suggests that it is targeting an Apple dependency ranged between 65-70%. There is plenty opportunity available for the company to add $250-350 million in revenue, which places its dependency in that range. We don't expect Apple to be 60% or less anytime soon, if ever.
What To Expect Only in the Next Few Years We are not expecting any significant revenue from either microphones or voice biometrics until at least the September quarter of 2020. We do expect yearly iPhone unit sales to effectively drift between 190-200 million during those coming 6 quarters. But we believe that Cirrus's revenue can, and will, grow in the next 6 quarters and beyond from significant opportunities with amplifier-based products. We believe that the earnings base case begins at $4 a share. We offer no stock price predictions.
Disclosure: I am/we are long CRUS.
